div.head: What is marked in the text
div.p: Inside its paragraphs and headings, a file may mark what the text says: the names of persons, places and events, the works it names, the statements it makes with their references and quotations, its formulae, the sources and parallels an edition gives, editorial remarks, dates and other languages, beside the scribal changes, gaps and unclear words of . In the application a node's text is plain text, and each mark is an annotation of a layer, anchored to a span of the text or a point in it (). The import splits the marked text into its plain text and its annotations; an export writes each annotation back in the same form, inline where it nests in the others, and in the standOff where it doesn't ().
Nothing in this part is required. Names of persons are common, since most files mark them; the rest is full: a file marks as much as its encoder claims.

div.head: Names and their records
div.p: A person's, a place's or an event's name is marked by persName, placeName or eventName, around the words of the text, and points to its record in ref, in one of three forms:

list.item: a placeholder: #new_, the kind of record, _, and a name of the encoder's own (#new_person_Arno), the same for every name of that record in the file;
an id in the file (#PERS.1234), where the record is listed in the file's standOff ();

div.p: The import makes a provisional record of each placeholder, one for all the names that share it, for the project to identify; it uses a permalink as given, without matching: a record merged since forwards to the record that replaced it, and a permalink that leads nowhere is reported. An export writes permalinks. In the preface of the Council of Mainz of 813, the king's envoys name themselves and the city:

egXML.p: Almifice reverentiae vestrae patefacimus nos humillimi famuli ac missi vestri, Hildibaldus scilicet sacri palatii archiepiscopus, Rihholfus et Arno archiepiscopi seu Bernharius, una cum reliquis coepiscopis atque abbatibus et caetero clero, quia venimus secundum iussionem vestram in civitatem Mogontiam …

div.p: An event is named the same way; the council names itself:

egXML.p: … Placuit itaque sancto concilio, ut ita discernantur, sicut in regula clericorum dictum est. …

div.p: A pointer to a record has one of the three forms, or fails the RelaxNG; a placeholder without its # is the commonest slip:
A record of a kind no name element fits, a diocese or a religious order, is marked by rs ().

dataSpec.desc: A pointer to a record: a placeholder (#new_person_…), an identifier in the file, or a permalink.

div.head: Works named
div.p: A work the text names, a book of the Bible, a Father's treatise, a council's canons, is marked by bibl, and points to the work's record in ref, in the forms of the names' records. The names inside it stay names. The council of 813 sets its bishops to read the Gospel and Gregory's pastoral book, and quotes Jerome's letter to Nepotian:

egXML.p: … legentes atque tractantes sanctum evangelium necnon epistolas et actus apostolorum, canones quoque ac diversa sanctorum patrum opuscula pastoralemque librum Gregorii cum caeteris sacris dogmatibus …

cit.ref: Tamen Hieronimus in epistola ad Nepotianum dicit:
cit.quote: Omnium Christianorum domos quasi proprias amare debemus, …

div.head: Statements, references, quotations, formulae
div.p: A statement cites an authority: it is a cit holding its reference, ref, the words that name the authority, and its quotation, quote, the words quoted. Whether the quotation is exact, or rightly attributed, doesn't change the form: the statements attributed to an authority are worth finding even where the attribution is wrong. A quotation names its source in source (); the words that introduce an authority by a set phrase ("ut lex dicit", "unde psalmista commemorat") are a formula, a seg typed formula, marked and not yet identified. Chapter II of the Council of Mainz, 813, is a chain of statements:

div.head: De spe habenda in Deum.
Cap.II
div.p: Spes vero in Deum firmiter a cunctis Christianis tenenda est. Unde psalmista commemorat: Sperate in eo omnis congregatio populi et reliqua, et iterum: Spera in Domino et fac bonitatem, … et apostolus: Spe enim salvi facti sumus.

The application reads a statement as three annotations: the reference, the quotation with its source, and the attribution, the source the reference claims. A reference whose claim sits in a heading rather than in the text's words is typed from_paratext, the only type a reference in the text takes; a link to a manuscript's images is typed iiif (). A quotation has no type: its source goes in source. A formula, and every other seg, has a type from its closed list.

constraintSpec.desc: A fragment's @next points to the next fragment in the file, of the same kind, whose @prev points back.

sch:assert.test: count($next) = 1 and local-name($next) = local-name() and normalize-space($next/@prev) = concat('#', @xml:id)

sch:rule.sch:assert: <>'s @next () points to the next fragment in the file, a <> whose @prev points back.

constraintSpec.desc: A fragment's @prev points to the previous fragment in the file, of the same kind, whose @next points back.

sch:assert.test: count($prev) = 1 and local-name($prev) = local-name() and normalize-space($prev/@next) = concat('#', @xml:id)

sch:rule.sch:assert: <>'s @prev () points to the previous fragment in the file, a <> whose @next points back.

constraintSpec.desc: Only the first fragment carries the attributes that describe the whole span; a later one carries its xml:id, @prev and @next, and the attributes the RelaxNG requires (a segment's type), with the first fragment's values.

sch:assert.test: every $a in $other satisfies (self::tei:seg and name($a) = 'type' and $a = $prev/@type)

sch:rule.sch:assert: <> is a later fragment (it has @prev): it carries only its xml:id, @prev and @next, and the span's other attributes () go on its first fragment.

constraintSpec.desc: A fragment's @next points to an element later in the file: the fragments follow the text's order.

sch:rule.sch:assert: <>'s @next () points to a fragment later in the file: the fragments follow the text's order.

div.head: Sources and the pointers' forms
div.p: A quotation's source, and a source note's, hold one pointer or more, separated by spaces, each in one of these forms:

list.item: a document's code (), alone (C.NIC-0325) or with a citation after an underscore, the canon or chapter of that document (C.NIC-0325_3, D.LEO-0447-414_11, COLL.Dach.ms-Brn-Burg-425_2.49); an underscore stands only there;
a work by its siglum in Gryson's Répertoire général des auteurs ecclésiastiques latins: the author, the work and the place cited (IS_ety_1.2.3, LEO_ep.167_6);
an SCTA resource, by its address (http://scta.info/resource/…).

div.p: The first three may begin with cf_ for a loose reference: a parallel or an echo rather than a quotation. The Collectio Dacheriana, in d'Achery's edition, echoes Ezekiel:

egXML.p: … uenia peccatorum fideliter præsumatur ab illo, qui non uult mortem peccatoris, sed ut conuertatur a perditione poenitendo, et saluatus miseratione Domini uiuat. …

div.p: The 73 books of the Bible have one code each. Their names are the Nova Vulgata's: the older Vulgate's I to IV Regum are 1SA, 2SA, 1KI and 2KI. solemne-tei lists prints the same table.

table.head: The Bible's books and their codes

div.p: The RelaxNG checks each pointer's form: an older code, an underscore inside a code, a book that isn't among the 73 or a verse that isn't a number fails. It doesn't check that the document or the verse exists; the import resolves each pointer into a relation to a canon, and reports what it can't resolve.

dataSpec.desc: A pointer to a source: a document's code, alone or with a citation after an underscore (C.NIC-0325_3); a Bible reference by book, chapter and verse (MAT_18_19, PHP_3_17-20); a Gryson siglum and the place cited (IS_ety_1.2.3); each may start with cf_ for a loose reference; or an SCTA resource. A code holds letters, digits, dots and hyphens; an underscore only separates a code from its citation.

div.head: Notes: sources, parallels, editorial remarks
div.p: A note in the text has a type, its layer:

list.item: source: where a passage comes from, as an edition says it: its words, and the codes of its sources in source;
parallel: a parallel elsewhere, an edition's "Cf." note;
editorial: a remark of the editor of the file, about the text or the transcription.

div.p: A note stands where its source puts it: at a point of a paragraph, or between paragraphs and divisions, where it annotates the division. The Council of Mainz, 813, in its chapter on the sacraments, cites Leo's decretal, which its editor identifies in a note, and the editor notes a parallel in a later council:

div.head: De sacramentis ecclesiae.
IIII
div.p: Sacramenta itaque baptismatis volumus, … sicut in decretis Leonis papae sub duobus continetur capitulis, in capitulo XL: Haec duo tempora, id est Pascha et Pentecosten, ad baptizandum a Romano pontifice legitima praefixa suntLeonis decreta c. 11 (Jaffe-K. n. 414)., …
div.note: Cf. concil. Mogunt. 847 c. 3; l. I. p. 176.

div.p: Where an edition's source note is only codes, they go in source, in the pointers' forms, and the note holds no words; codes left in a note's words are reported. A note holds words, or its codes, or both.
Notes typed links, authorities and extra belong to records (); in the text, they're errors.

The import keeps a source note's words and codes until the project resolves them into relations; a parallel and an editorial note keep their words, and an editorial note its author. An error of the source marked by sic, or an addition by supplied, is an editorial note too ().

constraintSpec.desc: In the text, a note's type is its layer.

sch:rule.sch:assert: A note in the text is typed source, parallel or editorial.

div.head: Dates
div.p: A date in the text is marked by date, in the one form of dates that records and relations use too: the wording as the text gives it, and its bounds in attributes. It names the calendar of its words: a day the text reckons in the Julian calendar says so, and its bounds give the Gregorian day (). The coded files mark none yet; the example is made up: V Idus Iunias is 9 June in the Julian calendar, 13 June in the Gregorian in 813.

div.head: What no element fits
div.p: TEI has an element for most of what the layers mark. For the rest:

list.item: a kind of mark with no element of its own is a seg, typed by its layer, and its term, where the layer has terms, in ana, pointing to a category of a taxonomy declared in the header;
a record of a kind no name element fits, a diocese or a religious order, is an rs, its kind in type and its record in ref, in the forms of the names' records;
a span that crosses others or the structure, a quotation over several paragraphs, is split into fragments;
a point, or a span that can't be marked inline at all, is marked by anchors, which a stand-off annotation points to.

div.head: Fragments
div.p: A span that can't nest where it stands is split into fragments, each nesting in its paragraph or heading, joined by next and prev: each fragment has an xml:id, each but the last points to the next by next, and each but the first to the one before by prev. The Collectio 400 capitulorum quotes two passages over several paragraphs; they're fragments. The rules:

list.item: each fragment's next and prev point to an element of the same kind in the file, which points back (fragment-next, fragment-prev);
next points to an element later in the file: the fragments follow the text's order, so a chain has one first fragment and no loop (fragment-order);

only the first fragment carries the attributes that describe the whole span, a quotation's source, a segment's ana, a name's ref; a later one carries its xml:id, prev and next, and a segment's type, which the RelaxNG requires on every segment, with the first fragment's value (fragment-attributes). So two fragments can't disagree.

div.head: Anchors
div.p: An anchor marks a point. A stand-off annotation, in the standOff's listAnnotation, points to one anchor, or to the range between two by TEI's range(). It's the form for what can't be marked inline at all; an export uses it for annotations that cross stronger ones (). A made-up example:

egXML.p: Placuit ut episcopi in ciuitatibus suis maneant.

annotation.note: A remark on the whole clause.
